paper.title: CaBP1 and 2 enable sustained CaV1.3 calcium currents and synaptic transmission in inner hair cells
paper.abstract: To encode continuous sound stimuli, the inner hair cell (IHC) ribbon synapses utilize calcium-binding proteins (CaBPs), which reduce the inactivation of their CaV1.3 calcium channels. Mutations in the CABP2 gene underlie non-syndromic autosomal recessive hearing loss DFNB93. Besides CaBP2, the structurally related CaBP1 is highly abundant in the IHCs. Here, we investigated how the two CaBPs cooperatively regulate IHC synaptic function. In Cabp1/2 double-knockout mice, we find strongly enhanced CaV1.3 inactivation, slowed recovery from inactivation and impaired sustained exocytosis. Already mild IHC activation further reduces the availability of channels to trigger synaptic transmission and may effectively silence synapses. Spontaneous and sound-evoked responses of spiral ganglion neurons in vivo are strikingly reduced and strongly depend on stimulation rates. Transgenic expression of CaBP2 leads to substantial recovery of IHC synaptic function and hearing sensitivity. We conclude that CaBP1 and 2 act together to suppress voltage- and calcium-dependent inactivation of IHC CaV1.3 channels in order to support sufficient rate of exocytosis and enable fast, temporally precise and indefatigable sound encoding.

nodes.label: CaBP1 and CaBP2 act together to provide sufficient attenuation of CaV1.3 channel…
nodes.claim: CaBP1 and CaBP2 act together to provide sufficient attenuation of CaV1.3 channel inactivation in IHCs to sustain Ca2+ currents and exocytosis required for temporally precise, indefatigable neurotransmission at the ribbon synapse, and their combined loss causes severe hearing impairment that can be partially rescued by viral CaBP2 gene delivery.
nodes.verbatim_quote: Together, they provide sufficient attenuation of channel inactivation to sustain Ca2+ currents and exocytosis required for temporally precise, indefatigable neurotransmission at this synapse.

strengths: The claim is supported by a comprehensive, multi-level dataset spanning biophysics (patch-clamp of Ca2+ currents), synaptic physiology (capacitance measurements of exocytosis), systems physiology (ABRs, DPOAEs), and in vivo single-unit recordings—a rare breadth for a single study.
The DKO phenotype is convincingly more severe than either single KO (sub-claim c1.1 rated strong), providing direct evidence for combined/synergistic function of CaBP1 and CaBP2.
Both VDI and CDI are quantified separately using Ba2+/Ca2+ substitution (Figure 2), with CDI approximately six-fold enhanced in DKO IHCs—a large and statistically robust effect (p < 0.0001).

The exocytosis data (sub-claim c1.2 rated strong) shows that sustained exocytosis is almost abolished at physiologically relevant holding potentials (–55 mV), directly linking channel inactivation to synaptic failure.

In vivo SGN recordings (sub-claim c1.3 rated strong) demonstrate dramatically reduced spontaneous and evoked spike rates with enhanced adaptation, providing a clear functional correlate of the cellular phenotype.

The viral rescue experiment (sub-claim c1.5 rated strong) provides a causal test: re-expression of CaBP2 partially restores Ca2+ currents, exocytosis, and ABR thresholds/amplitudes, strengthening the causal chain from CaBP loss to hearing impairment.
The authors appropriately use language such as 'partially overlap' and note incomplete rescue, which tempers the overall claim.
weaknesses: EVIDENTIAL gap inherited from sub-claim c1.2: The mechanism by which exocytosis efficiency is reduced beyond what diminished QCa would predict is entirely unknown and only speculated upon. This weakens the 'exocytosis required for neurotransmission' component of the root claim, as the full mechanistic chain is not established.

EVIDENTIAL gap inherited from sub-claim c1.6 (rated moderate): The claim that channel inactivation drives the in vivo phenotype is an extrapolation from ex vivo recordings at room temperature to physiological conditions in vivo. No direct in vivo measurement of channel inactivation state was performed.

INFERENTIAL gap from sub-claim c1.4 (rated moderate): The claim of 'partial overlap' of CaBP1/2 function is inferred from the DKO-worse-than-SKO pattern, but no molecular-level evidence (e.g., binding competition, co-immunoprecipitation, structure-function analysis) demonstrates functional overlap at the protein level.

Approximately half of DKO animals showed reduced DPOAEs (sub-claim c1.3.3, rated moderate), meaning the hearing impairment may not be purely due to IHC synaptic dysfunction—some contribution from impaired cochlear amplification cannot be excluded, complicating the clean narrative.

Key electrophysiology was performed at room temperature with non-physiological extracellular Ca2+ concentrations (1.3 or 2 mM). CDI magnitude is temperature-sensitive, introducing uncertainty about the quantitative relevance of the inactivation parameters under physiological conditions.

Comparison to single KOs partly relies on previously published data (Picher, 2017; Yang et al., 2018) acquired under potentially different experimental conditions, which could confound the quantitative comparison in Figure 1C.

Severe selection bias in SGN recordings (0.3 vs 2.5 neurons/hour) means detected DKO neurons likely overrepresent the least-affected population; the true in vivo phenotype may be even worse, but equally, characterization of the most severely affected neurons is absent.

The paradoxical finding that recovery from 500-ms step inactivation is fastest in DKO IHCs (sub-claim c1.6.2) complicates the narrative of impaired recovery, and the offered explanation (faster Ca2+ clearance due to less Ca2+ entry) remains speculative without supporting Ca2+ imaging data.

Viral rescue is incomplete—ABR thresholds do not fully recover, and multiple non-exclusive explanations are offered (inadequate expression, irreversible developmental changes, absence of CaBP1) without the ability to distinguish among them.

The claim uses the phrase 'temporally precise, indefatigable neurotransmission,' which implies a degree of mechanistic clarity and completeness that slightly overstates the evidence, though the authors do qualify with 'partially' in rescue contexts.
alternative_interpretations: The hearing impairment could partly reflect impaired cochlear amplification in the subset of DKO animals with reduced DPOAEs, rather than being solely attributable to IHC CaV1.3 inactivation.

The exocytosis efficiency deficit beyond reduced QCa could indicate CaBP roles entirely independent of CaV1.3 modulation—e.g., direct effects on vesicle priming, otoferlin function, or endocytosis—meaning the claim that CaBPs act primarily through 'attenuation of channel inactivation' may understate their broader synaptic roles.

Developmental compensation or maladaptation (e.g., reduced BK channel expression, altered synaptic morphology) may contribute to the phenotype independently of acute CaV1.3 inactivation, complicating the direct causal inference.

The incomplete rescue by CaBP2 overexpression could reflect off-target effects of viral transduction or CaBP2 overexpression toxicity rather than simply the absence of CaBP1, as discussed by Oestreicher et al. (2021).
required_assumptions: Room-temperature, non-physiological Ca2+ concentration patch-clamp data can be reasonably extrapolated to in vivo IHC physiology.
The phenotype of the DKO is primarily attributable to IHC CaV1.3 dysfunction rather than to effects on SGNs, OHCs, or other cochlear cell types.
CaBP1 and CaBP2 act primarily at the level of CaV1.3 channels, and the enhanced inactivation is the dominant mechanism causing hearing impairment.
The viral rescue experiment delivers CaBP2 at appropriate levels and timing to meaningfully test reversibility, and incomplete rescue reflects biological rather than technical limitations.
Single KO data from prior publications (Picher, 2017; Yang et al., 2018) are sufficiently comparable in methodology to the current DKO data for valid quantitative comparison.
evaluation.notes: The root claim is a composite of six sub-claims spanning channel biophysics, exocytosis, in vivo physiology, functional overlap, rescue, and recovery kinetics. Most sub-claims are rated strong, but two (c1.4 and c1.6) are moderate, introducing evidential and inferential gaps that propagate to the root. The overall claim is well-supported but not without meaningful gaps, particularly regarding the mechanistic specificity of CaBP action (channel inactivation vs. other synaptic roles) and the extrapolation from ex vivo to in vivo. The authors generally calibrate their language appropriately, using qualifiers like 'partially' and acknowledging unknowns, which prevents the claim from being clearly overclaimed despite the gaps.

nodes.label: Combined loss of CaBP1 and CaBP2 causes dramatically enhanced CaV1.3 inactivatio…
nodes.claim: Combined loss of CaBP1 and CaBP2 causes dramatically enhanced CaV1.3 inactivation in IHCs, significantly stronger than in either single knockout, affecting both voltage-dependent and calcium-dependent inactivation.
nodes.verbatim_quote: Employing 500-ms long depolarization steps to maximal Ca2+-current potential (−25 to –15 mV) revealed pronounced inactivation of CaV1.3 channels in the DKO IHCs.

strengths: Direct electrophysiological measurements comparing DKO to single KOs and WT with appropriate statistical analysis (p < 0.0001 for both VDI and CDI)
Quantification of both VDI and CDI separately using Ba2+/Ca2+ substitution paradigm following established methodology (Tadross et al., 2010)
CDI approximately 6-fold and VDI approximately 2-fold larger in DKO vs WT provides clear evidence of dramatic enhancement
Multiple convergent measures: 500-ms step inactivation, train stimuli, and Ba2+/Ca2+ experiments all consistent
All supporting sub-claims (c1.1.1–c1.1.5) rated as strong evidence, and they logically compose into the parent claim
Partial rescue by CaBP2 re-expression provides causal support for the CaBP1/2-dependence of the phenotype
weaknesses: Recordings at room temperature and non-physiological extracellular Ca2+ concentrations (2 mM for VDI/CDI separation); the magnitude of CDI in particular is temperature-sensitive
Comparison to single KOs relies partly on previously published data from different studies (Yang et al., 2018; Picher, 2017) with potentially different methodological nuances
Cabp2 KO data acquired at different tonotopic positions (lower apex to mid-cochlea vs apex for others), introducing a potential confound in cross-genotype comparisons

The unexpected hyperpolarized shift in activation voltage contradicts predictions from heterologous systems and is left unexplained, suggesting the DKO IHC environment is complex and not fully characterized
Sample sizes for specific Ba2+/Ca2+ experiments are only partially reported (n=13 for DKO in 2 mM condition)
alternative_interpretations: Secondary changes in CaV1.3 splice variant expression, auxiliary subunit composition, or other modulators in DKO IHCs could contribute to the enhanced inactivation beyond the direct loss of CaBP-mediated CDI suppression
The enhanced VDI component could reflect altered channel conformational states due to chronic absence of CaBP binding rather than acute loss of CaBP modulation
required_assumptions: Room temperature recordings reflect the direction (if not exact magnitude) of inactivation differences at physiological temperature
Previously published single KO data are reasonably comparable to current DKO data despite being from different studies
Ba2+ substitution adequately isolates VDI from CDI in native IHC CaV1.3 channels
evaluation.notes: The claim is well-supported by multiple lines of evidence. The main caveat is reliance on cross-study comparisons for the 'stronger than either single KO' component, though the magnitude of the DKO effect is large enough that this is unlikely to be an artifact of methodological differences.

nodes.label: The combined absence of CaBP1 and 2 severely impairs IHC synaptic exocytosis, al…
nodes.claim: The combined absence of CaBP1 and 2 severely impairs IHC synaptic exocytosis, almost abolishing sustained exocytosis and reducing exocytosis efficiency beyond what can be attributed to reduced Ca2+ influx, especially under physiologically relevant conditions.
nodes.verbatim_quote: we demonstrate that the combined absence of CaBP1 and 2 almost abolishes sustained, and, upon increased hair cell synaptic activity, the fast component of exocytosis.

strengths: Systematic capacitance measurements across multiple stimulus durations clearly show preserved fast exocytosis but severely impaired sustained exocytosis
Exocytosis efficiency analysis (ΔCm/QCa) reveals impairment beyond what reduced Ca2+ influx alone would explain, with appropriate statistical analysis
Experiments at multiple holding potentials (-85, -65, -55 mV) strengthen the claim by showing aggravation under more physiological conditions
Rescue by CaBP2 re-expression supports causal attribution to CaBP1/2 loss
Comparison to single KO phenotypes (normal exocytosis in Cabp2-KO, no defects in Cabp1-KO) contextualizes the DKO finding
weaknesses: The mechanism underlying reduced exocytosis efficiency is unknown—sub-claim c1.2.2 (rated moderate) identifies no direct experimental evidence for any specific mechanism, creating an evidential gap for the 'beyond reduced Ca2+ influx' component
No direct investigation of coupling between CaV1.3 channels and synaptic vesicles, or effects on otoferlin/vesicle replenishment machinery
The uncontrolled sine wave during capacitance measurements adds channel activation that varies between genotypes, complicating quantitative interpretation
Comparisons to single KO exocytosis are from different studies with different conditions, as acknowledged in sub-claim c1.2.4
The 'almost abolishing sustained exocytosis' language in the abstract is more absolute than the data at -85 mV show—it is primarily at -55 mV holding potential that sustained exocytosis is near-zero
alternative_interpretations: Reduced exocytosis efficiency could reflect enhanced endocytosis rather than impaired exocytosis per se

The additional exocytosis deficit beyond QCa reduction could be due to altered Ca2+ channel-vesicle coupling distance resulting from chronic channel dysfunction rather than a direct CaBP role in exocytosis
At more depolarized holding potentials, the apparent 'loss' of sustained exocytosis could partly reflect pre-depolarization depletion of vesicle pools by tonic Ca2+ entry
required_assumptions: Capacitance measurements accurately reflect exocytosis (not confounded by changes in endocytosis kinetics)
QCa is a reasonable proxy for the Ca2+ signal driving exocytosis at individual active zones
The exocytosis efficiency metric (ΔCm/QCa) is valid despite whole-cell averaging over heterogeneous active zones
evaluation.notes: The claim is appropriately hedged in the results ('almost abolishes') and discussion ('reduced efficiency...beyond QCa'). The authors correctly note the caveat that mechanisms are unknown. The claim that this 'was observed neither in Cabp1 nor in Cabp2 single KO animals' is well-supported but the comparison is somewhat compromised by cross-study methodology differences.

nodes.label: CaBP1/2-DKO animals exhibit severe hearing impairment with drastically degraded …
nodes.claim: CaBP1/2-DKO animals exhibit severe hearing impairment with drastically degraded sound encoding by spiral ganglion neurons, far exceeding the phenotype of either single knockout.
nodes.verbatim_quote: Already in young (3- to 4-week-old) Cabp1/2-DKO animals, ABR thresholds were highly elevated, with tone bursts up to a maximum intensity of 90 dB SPL barely eliciting any ABR response.

strengths: Multi-level evidence: ABR thresholds, ABR amplitudes, single-unit SGN recordings all converge on severe hearing impairment
Quantitative ABR data shows near-absent responses to tone bursts up to 90 dB SPL and severely elevated click thresholds
Single-unit data reveals dramatically reduced spontaneous and evoked spike rates, increased latency and jitter, and enhanced adaptation
Progressive worsening documented between 3-4 and 7-13 weeks
DPOAEs largely preserved in many animals, localizing the deficit to IHC synapse/neural level
Multiple supporting sub-claims (c1.3.1-c1.3.7) rated strong, providing robust compositional support
weaknesses: Severe selection bias in SGN recordings: 0.3 vs 2.5 neurons/hour yield means detected DKO neurons likely overrepresent the least-affected units, so the in vivo phenotype may be even worse than documented

Approximately half of DKO animals showed reduced DPOAEs, slightly weakening the claim that the phenotype is purely synaptic/neural—some OHC contribution cannot be excluded (sub-claim c1.3.3, rated moderate)
Ceiling artifact in tone burst ABR thresholds (assigned 100 dB when exceeding 90 dB max) underestimates true threshold elevation
The 'far exceeding the phenotype of either single knockout' component relies on cross-study comparisons with the published single KO phenotypes
BK channel reduction mechanism is entirely speculative (sub-claim c1.3.6), though this is a secondary finding
alternative_interpretations: Some of the hearing impairment, particularly at later ages, could involve OHC dysfunction given the partially reduced DPOAEs in a subset of animals
Reduced SGN spontaneous rates could reflect loss of caldendrin (CaBP1 isoform) function in SGNs rather than solely presynaptic IHC dysfunction
The severe ABR phenotype could partly reflect immature IHC development (given BK channel changes and occasional SK2 retention) rather than purely acute channel inactivation
required_assumptions: ABR threshold elevation primarily reflects IHC synaptic dysfunction rather than combined IHC and OHC deficits
The single KO phenotype data from previous studies are valid comparators despite methodological differences
Low SGN recording yield reflects true absence of spiking rather than technical difficulty in accessing neurons in these animals
evaluation.notes: The claim is well-calibrated—the authors use appropriate language ('severe hearing impairment') and acknowledge the DPOAE findings. The SGN recording bias is honestly reported. The composite evidence from ABR, SGN recordings, and cellular physiology provides strong multi-level support.

nodes.label: The functions of CaBP1 and CaBP2 partially overlap at the IHC ribbon synapse, su…
nodes.claim: The functions of CaBP1 and CaBP2 partially overlap at the IHC ribbon synapse, such that loss of either one can be largely compensated by the other, but CaBP2 exerts more potent suppression of CaV1.3 inactivation.
nodes.verbatim_quote: This suggests that the sole loss of either CaBP1 or 2, can be largely compensated by the other of the two CaBP members.

strengths: The logic is sound: mild single KO phenotypes combined with severe DKO phenotype is consistent with partial redundancy
CaBP1 KO has normal hearing initially while CaBP2 KO has progressive impairment, and DKO has severe early impairment—this pattern supports overlapping but unequal contributions
The argument that CaBP2 is more potent is supported by the observation that CaBP2 loss alone causes hearing impairment while CaBP1 loss does not (initially)
weaknesses: Inferential gap: the claim of 'partial overlap' is an interpretation of the DKO-worse-than-SKO pattern, but no direct evidence demonstrates functional overlap at the molecular level (e.g., competition for binding sites, redundant interactions with CaV1.3)
No new expression data generated; reliance on previously published work (Yang et al., 2016) for expression patterns (sub-claim c1.4.1, rated moderate)
The distinction between 'concentration-limited compensation' and 'distinct properties' is entirely speculative with no experiments to distinguish them (sub-claim c1.4.2, rated moderate)
The dismissal of SGN dysfunction as 'rather unlikely' may be premature given that caldendrin (CaBP1 isoform) is expressed in SGNs and its function there is unknown (sub-claim c1.4.3, rated moderate)
No CaBP1 overexpression experiments were performed, which would directly test whether CaBP1 can functionally substitute for CaBP2
Three of three supporting sub-claims are rated moderate, pulling down the parent claim's support
alternative_interpretations: Rather than 'partial overlap,' CaBP1 and CaBP2 could have entirely distinct functions that happen to converge on the same downstream phenotype (CaV1.3 inactivation) through different mechanisms
CaBP1 may primarily regulate CaV1.3 at rest/low activity while CaBP2 during sustained activity—this would appear as 'overlap' in the DKO but reflect division of labor rather than true redundancy
The DKO phenotype being worse than either SKO could reflect loss of total CaBP buffering capacity rather than overlap in specific CaV1.3 modulatory functions
required_assumptions: CaBP1 and CaBP2 interact with the same molecular targets (CaV1.3 channels) in IHCs
The hearing phenotype is primarily driven by IHC synapse dysfunction rather than combined IHC and SGN effects
Previously published single KO data are valid comparators for the current DKO study
evaluation.notes: This is primarily an interpretive claim rather than one with direct experimental support. The pattern is consistent with partial overlap, but the specific molecular mechanism is not addressed. The claim is appropriately hedged in the paper with qualifiers like 'partially overlap' and acknowledgment that the mechanism is unknown.

nodes.label: Viral delivery of CaBP2 coding sequence substantially rescues auditory function …
nodes.claim: Viral delivery of CaBP2 coding sequence substantially rescues auditory function in DKO animals, restoring Ca2+ currents, IHC exocytosis, and ABR responses, supporting gene therapy as a viable treatment for CaBP-related deafness.
nodes.verbatim_quote: These experiments revealed a substantial recovery of hearing, which may be related to the successful restoration of Ca2+ currents and IHC exocytosis upon transgenic expression of CaBP2.

strengths: Multi-level rescue demonstrated: Ca2+ current inactivation, exocytosis, ABR thresholds, wave I amplitudes, and wave I latency all improve with CaBP2 re-expression
Widespread transduction documented by eGFP immunofluorescence across tonotopic regions
Rescue of exocytosis efficiency specifically supports the claim that CaBP2 restores function beyond just Ca2+ influx
ABR wave I amplitudes in rescued animals are very large, indicating robust functional recovery
The partial (not complete) nature of rescue is honestly reported and appropriately discussed
Supporting sub-claims c1.5.1, c1.5.2, c1.5.3, and c1.5.5 are rated strong
weaknesses: Rescue is incomplete: ABR thresholds do not fully recover to WT levels, leaving uncertainty about the ultimate therapeutic potential
The reasons for incomplete rescue are speculative—multiple non-exclusive explanations offered without ability to distinguish (sub-claim c1.5.4, rated moderate)
Very large wave I in rescued animals could reflect overexpression-driven enhancement rather than normalization, complicating interpretation of 'rescue'
Lower eGFP expression toward cochlear base suggests tonotopic variation in rescue efficacy that is not fully characterized
Only the CaBP2 L-isoform was used for rescue, while the CaBP2-alt isoform may be the most abundant in IHCs (Yang et al., 2016)—this could explain incomplete rescue
The gene therapy claim ('viable treatment') is arguably an inferential leap from mouse rescue data to human therapeutic applicability
Train stimulus data came from cells with lower-than-average inactivation (0.36 vs 0.47), potentially biasing the rescue assessment for this specific measure
alternative_interpretations: The very large wave I in rescued animals could reflect CaBP1-KO-like hyperexcitability (as seen in young Cabp1 KOs) superimposed on CaBP2 rescue, rather than true normalization
Incomplete threshold rescue could indicate that CaBP1 has unique functions that CaBP2 cannot substitute, rather than insufficient CaBP2 expression
The rescue could be selecting for a subset of IHCs/synapses with adequate CaBP2 expression while leaving others dysfunctional
required_assumptions: The CaBP2 L-isoform can substitute functionally for the endogenous CaBP2-alt and CaBP1 isoforms at IHC synapses
The PHP.eB capsid provides adequate and sustained expression in IHCs without significant toxicity
The partial rescue reflects a translatable therapeutic effect rather than a ceiling limited by the mouse model or viral vector system
evaluation.notes: The claim is well-calibrated—the authors use 'substantial recovery' and 'partially restored' rather than claiming complete rescue. The gene therapy framing in the discussion is appropriately tentative ('may be targeted by gene therapy in the future'). However, the very large wave I in rescued animals warrants more discussion, as it could indicate pathological overexcitability rather than normalization.

nodes.label: In vivo, the absence of CaBP1 and 2 drives a large fraction of IHC CaV1.3 channe…
nodes.claim: In vivo, the absence of CaBP1 and 2 drives a large fraction of IHC CaV1.3 channels into a state of prolonged inactivation with very slow recovery, especially upon sustained or repeated stimulation, which does not support sufficient neurotransmission for sound encoding.
nodes.verbatim_quote: We propose that in vivo in the absence of CaBP1 and 2 a large fraction of IHC CaV1.3 channels are in a state of prolonged inactivation.

strengths: Recovery experiments with two distinct conditioning paradigms (500-ms step and 2-min sine wave) provide direct evidence for slowed recovery kinetics
Double exponential recovery in DKO vs single exponential in WT after 2-min sine wave directly supports the 'deep-state' inactivation concept
In vivo SGN data showing recovery of onset rates only at very low stimulus repetition rates (0.5-0.2 Hz) provides convergent physiological evidence
Reduced spontaneous spiking in DKO SGNs is consistent with steady-state inactivation even in silence
The holding potential experiments (Figure 3D,E) showing aggravation with increased tonic depolarization support the in vivo extrapolation
Sub-claim c1.6.1 (recovery data) and c1.6.3 (activity-dependent deterioration) rated strong
weaknesses: The claim is fundamentally an extrapolation from ex vivo to in vivo—no direct in vivo measurement of channel inactivation state was performed

The paradoxical finding that recovery after 500-ms step is fastest in DKO IHCs complicates the narrative and is explained speculatively via Ca2+ clearance hypothesis with no experimental validation (sub-claim c1.6.2, rated moderate)
No Ca2+ imaging was performed to support the Ca2+ clearance hypothesis
The 2-min sine wave is an imperfect proxy for in vivo stimulation; actual IHC receptor potentials during sound have different frequency content, amplitude, and duration
Sample sizes for recovery experiments are not explicitly stated in the text
The concept of 'deep-state inactivation' is borrowed from NaV/KV literature and may not directly apply to CaV1.3 channels in native IHCs
alternative_interpretations: Reduced spontaneous spiking could reflect postsynaptic changes (e.g., reduced AMPA receptor availability due to chronic under-stimulation) rather than presynaptic channel inactivation
The low SGN recording yield could partly reflect technical factors (e.g., altered cochlear anatomy) rather than purely reflecting inactivated channels
In vivo, other compensatory mechanisms (e.g., modulatory input from efferents, changes in IHC resting potential) might partially mitigate channel inactivation
required_assumptions: Ex vivo channel inactivation and recovery kinetics can be meaningfully extrapolated to in vivo conditions
The IHC resting potential in vivo is sufficiently depolarized to cause significant steady-state inactivation of CaV1.3 channels in the absence of CaBP1/2
Spontaneous IHC activity and sound-evoked stimulation produce sufficient Ca2+ influx to drive channels into prolonged inactivation states in vivo
evaluation.notes: The claim is appropriately presented as a proposal ('We propose that in vivo...') rather than a definitive conclusion. The supporting in vivo SGN data showing stimulus-rate-dependent recovery is the strongest indirect evidence for this claim. The paradoxical recovery finding after 500-ms steps (faster in DKO) actually weakens the straightforward interpretation but the authors discuss this thoughtfully. Overall, the in vivo extrapolation is reasonable but remains inferential.

nodes.label: Both VDI and CDI of IHC CaV1.3 channels are significantly enhanced in DKO IHCs, …
nodes.claim: Both VDI and CDI of IHC CaV1.3 channels are significantly enhanced in DKO IHCs, approximately two-fold and six-fold larger than in WT, respectively.
nodes.verbatim_quote: The lack of CaBP1 and 2 significantly enhanced both, VDI and CDI of IHC CaV1.3 channels, which were approx. two and six times larger than those in WT IHCs

strengths: Direct quantitative measurements using Ba2+ and Ca2+ currents with established analytical framework (Tadross et al., 2010) to separately quantify VDI and CDI
Clear statistical significance (p < 0.0001, Student's t-test) for both VDI and CDI differences
Specific numerical values provided: VDI 0.30 vs 0.13 and CDI 0.65 vs 0.11 in DKO vs WT, supporting the ~2x and ~6x claims
The sub-claim c1.1.1.1 is rated strong with calibrated claim-evidence match
weaknesses: Recordings performed at room temperature with 2 mM extracellular Ca2+, which may not reflect physiological conditions; the magnitude of CDI may differ at body temperature
Sample sizes for these specific Ba2+ vs Ca2+ comparison experiments are not explicitly stated in the main text excerpt (n=13 for DKO 2mM condition mentioned in supplement)
No dose-response or graded analysis—only full DKO vs WT comparison
alternative_interpretations: The enhanced inactivation could partially reflect compensatory changes in auxiliary subunit composition or splice variant expression, not purely the direct absence of CaBP-mediated modulation
required_assumptions: Ba2+ currents faithfully report VDI without significant CDI component
The Tadross et al. (2010) analytical framework validly separates VDI and CDI in this preparation
Room temperature recordings adequately reflect the qualitative pattern of inactivation changes
evaluation.notes: The approximately two-fold and six-fold differences are well-supported by the reported values. The six-fold CDI increase is particularly striking given that CDI was previously thought to be minimally affected by CaBP2 alone (Picher, 2017).

nodes.label: CaV1.3 inactivation in DKO IHCs is significantly stronger than in either Cabp1 o…
nodes.claim: CaV1.3 inactivation in DKO IHCs is significantly stronger than in either Cabp1 or Cabp2 single knockouts under comparable conditions.
nodes.verbatim_quote: This was significantly stronger when compared to the inactivation observed in the IHCs of Cabp1 or Cabp2 single KOs in similar conditions

strengths: Figure 1C directly compares DKO data with previously published Cabp1 KO (Yang et al., 2018) and Cabp2 KO (Picher, 2017) data acquired under comparable conditions
Additional comparison to Cabp2 KO data at physiological temperature (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D) further substantiates the claim
The comparison uses fraction of remaining current after 500-ms depolarization, a standard metric
weaknesses: Comparisons rely partially on previously published data from different studies, which may have subtle methodological differences despite nominally comparable conditions
Cabp2 KO data were acquired at different tonotopic positions (lower apex to mid-cochlea) due to mild phenotype at the apex, introducing a confound in the comparison

No direct statistical comparison between DKO and single KO data is explicitly reported in the text excerpt (it says 'significantly stronger' but formal statistics for this specific comparison are not detailed)
alternative_interpretations: The enhanced inactivation in DKO could reflect non-additive interactions (e.g., compensatory upregulation of one CaBP when the other is absent that is lost in the DKO)
required_assumptions: Recording conditions across different studies are sufficiently similar to allow valid comparison
Tonotopic differences do not confound the comparison with Cabp2 KO data
evaluation.notes: The comparison with single KOs is critical for the partial redundancy argument. The different tonotopic positions for Cabp2 KO data are a known limitation acknowledged by the authors.

nodes.label: The voltage dependence of CaV1.3 activation is shifted toward more hyperpolarize…
nodes.claim: The voltage dependence of CaV1.3 activation is shifted toward more hyperpolarized values in DKO IHCs, which is the opposite of what would be expected from heterologous expression data.
nodes.verbatim_quote: We observed a slight shift in the voltage dependence of CaV1.3 activation toward more hyperpolarized values...This finding is somewhat surprising as the opposite would be expected based on data from heterologous expression systems

strengths: Clear quantitative data: V0.5 of -33.6 ± 0.5 mV in DKO vs -30.9 ± 0.5 mV in WT, with p < 0.0001
Slope differences also statistically significant (7.6 ± 0.1 vs 7.1 ± 0.1, p < 0.0001)
Authors are transparent about this being 'somewhat surprising' and opposite to heterologous expression predictions (Haeseleer et al., 2004; Picher, 2017; Shaltiel et al., 2012)
Sub-claim c1.1.3.1 is rated strong/calibrated
weaknesses: The hyperpolarized shift is relatively small (~2.7 mV) though statistically significant
Authors cannot explain the discrepancy with heterologous expression systems and acknowledge possible confounds from splice variant changes or auxiliary subunit alterations
The unexplained direction of the shift raises questions about whether additional molecular changes have occurred in the DKO that are unrelated to CaBP function per se
alternative_interpretations: Compensatory upregulation of short CaV1.3 splice variants (which have more hyperpolarized activation) could explain the shift independently of direct CaBP effects
Changes in auxiliary beta subunit expression or other modulatory proteins could contribute
required_assumptions: The shift reflects a genuine biophysical change rather than a systematic recording artifact
evaluation.notes: This finding, while well-documented, somewhat complicates the overall narrative. The authors handle it appropriately by not over-interpreting it.

nodes.label: Maximal Ca2+-current amplitudes in DKO IHCs are comparable to controls upon shor…
nodes.claim: Maximal Ca2+-current amplitudes in DKO IHCs are comparable to controls upon short depolarization steps, indicating that channel expression is not grossly reduced.
nodes.verbatim_quote: Short stimuli at different potentials revealed maximal Ca2+-current amplitudes in the IHCs of DKO mice that were comparable to controls

strengths: I-V relationships (Figure 1E) directly show comparable peak amplitudes between DKO and WT
Consistent with normal CaV1.3 immunofluorescence clustering (Figure 5A)
Important control demonstrating that the phenotype is about channel gating kinetics, not expression level
weaknesses: Slight reduction in Ca2+ current amplitudes noted in PHP.eB-Cabp2 transduced IHCs (Figure 1E), which somewhat complicates interpretation
Peak current comparison uses short steps that may not fully reveal differences if a fraction of channels is already in fast inactivation
alternative_interpretations: Even with comparable peak currents, surface expression could be slightly altered if individual channel conductance differs, though this is unlikely for the same alpha subunit
required_assumptions: Short depolarizing steps activate channels before significant inactivation occurs
Peak current amplitude is a valid proxy for the number of available channels
evaluation.notes: This is a standard and well-executed control that strengthens the overall argument.

nodes.label: CaV1.3 channel clustering and ribbon synapse counts appear normal in DKO IHCs, i…
nodes.claim: CaV1.3 channel clustering and ribbon synapse counts appear normal in DKO IHCs, indicating that the inactivation phenotype is not due to altered channel localization or synapse number.
nodes.verbatim_quote: Immunolabeling of the organs of Corti indicated normal presynaptic CaV1.3 clustering with no apparent change in size or shape of the clusters...and comparable abundance of ribbon synapses

strengths: CaV1.3 immunofluorescence shows normal clustering with no apparent change in size or shape (Figure 5A)
Ribbon synapse counts are nearly identical: 12.9 ± 0.2 vs 12.8 ± 0.8 in WT and DKO
Both pre- and postsynaptic markers used for synapse identification
Sub-claim c1.1.5.1 rated strong/calibrated
weaknesses: Assessment only at 3 weeks of age; later time points might show synapse loss
N (number of animals) not explicitly stated for synapse counts in the text excerpt
'Normal clustering' is based on qualitative appearance without quantitative cluster size analysis
Increased immunofluorescence intensity of synaptic markers (Figure 5G) suggests some synaptic remodeling is occurring, even if counts are normal
alternative_interpretations: Normal synapse numbers at 3 weeks could mask subtle ultrastructural changes visible only by electron microscopy
required_assumptions: Immunofluorescence adequately reports channel localization and synapse number
3-week time point is representative
evaluation.notes: The increased immunofluorescence intensity of pre- and postsynaptic markers (c1.3.5) somewhat modifies this claim—while counts and clustering are normal, the synaptic composition is not entirely unchanged.

nodes.label: Sustained exocytosis (100–200 ms depolarizations) is significantly reduced in DK…
nodes.claim: Sustained exocytosis (100–200 ms depolarizations) is significantly reduced in DKO IHCs while the readily releasable pool evoked by short stimuli is comparable to WT when held at –85 mV.
nodes.verbatim_quote: In response to short stimuli [primarily recruiting the readily releasable pool (RRP) of vesicles], increases in capacitance were comparable, while long stimuli (reporting sustained exocytosis) evoked significantly smaller responses in the CaBP1/2-deficient IHCs

strengths: Standard membrane capacitance measurements with multiple stimulus durations provide a systematic comparison
Statistical significance achieved for sustained exocytosis (p < 0.05 for 20 ms, p < 0.001 for 100 and 200 ms)
Correlation with reduced QCa for longer pulses provides mechanistic consistency
Sub-claim c1.2.1.1 rated strong/calibrated
weaknesses: Sample sizes for individual time points not explicitly stated in text excerpt
Recordings at -85 mV holding potential may underestimate the in vivo phenotype, as the authors themselves later demonstrate (Figure 3D)
Comparable RRP at -85 mV may not hold at more physiological holding potentials
alternative_interpretations: Comparable RRP exocytosis at short durations could reflect sufficient Ca2+ entry during the first few milliseconds before inactivation becomes significant, rather than truly normal vesicle pool status
required_assumptions: Membrane capacitance measurements faithfully report exocytosis
-85 mV holding potential provides a meaningful starting condition for comparison
evaluation.notes: The authors appropriately note that -85 mV recordings underestimate the phenotype and proceed to test at more physiological potentials.

nodes.label: The reduction in sustained exocytosis cannot be completely explained by diminish…
nodes.claim: The reduction in sustained exocytosis cannot be completely explained by diminished Ca2+ influx, suggesting an additional impairment in exo- or endocytic processes of unknown mechanism.
nodes.verbatim_quote: calculating exocytosis efficiency revealed that the reduction in sustained exocytosis cannot completely be explained by the diminished Ca2+ influx

strengths: The efficiency calculation (ΔCm/QCa) is a standard approach to assess whether exocytosis changes simply track Ca2+ influx changes
Reduced efficiency was rescued by CaBP2 expression, linking it to CaBP absence rather than a general IHC health issue
The claim is appropriately hedged ('suggests an additional impairment...the underlying mechanism of which is currently unknown')
weaknesses: Evidential gap inherited from sub-claim c1.2.2.1 (rated weak): no direct experimental evidence for CaBP-CaMKII-otoferlin pathway or any other specific mechanism
No interaction studies between CaBPs and synaptic proteins were performed
The efficiency metric assumes linear Ca2+-exocytosis coupling, which may not hold across different Ca2+ entry conditions
Endocytic contributions to capacitance changes during long pulses could confound the efficiency calculation
alternative_interpretations: Reduced efficiency could reflect enhanced endocytosis rather than impaired exocytosis
Changes in Ca2+ microdomain characteristics (due to altered inactivation kinetics) rather than total QCa may better predict exocytosis
CaBPs might affect Ca2+ channel-vesicle coupling distance, which would change the relationship between bulk QCa and local [Ca2+] at release sites
required_assumptions: ΔCm/QCa is a valid metric for exocytosis efficiency
Linear relationship between Ca2+ charge and exocytosis is expected
Endocytosis does not significantly confound capacitance measurements at these time scales
evaluation.notes: The claim is appropriately cautious but the mechanistic gap is significant. The authors' speculation about CaMKII and otoferlin is interesting but entirely unsupported.

nodes.label: The exocytosis phenotype dramatically worsens at more physiological holding pote…
nodes.claim: The exocytosis phenotype dramatically worsens at more physiological holding potentials (–55 mV), resulting in complete loss of sustained exocytosis in DKO IHCs.
nodes.verbatim_quote: Raising the holding voltage to –55 mV resulted in a significant reduction in the maximal Ca2+ currents, which was more pronounced in the CaBP1/2-deficient IHCs...which in DKO animals resulted in a complete loss of sustained exocytosis

strengths: Systematic comparison across holding potentials (-85, -65, -55 mV) with clear progressive worsening
60% vs 25% reduction in peak Ca2+ current at -55 mV in DKO vs WT (p < 0.005) provides a compelling quantitative comparison
Further confirmed by sine wave amplitude manipulation showing intermediate phenotype
Statistical significance for exocytosis loss (p < 0.005)
Sub-claim c1.2.3.1 rated strong/calibrated
weaknesses: The claim of 'complete loss' of sustained exocytosis should be interpreted cautiously—small responses may fall below detection threshold
The sine wave during capacitance measurements adds uncontrolled additional channel activation
The exact resting potential of IHCs in vivo is debated, so the physiological relevance of -55 mV vs -65 mV is uncertain
alternative_interpretations: The worsening at -55 mV could partly reflect steady-state inactivation reached during the holding period rather than activity-dependent inactivation per se
required_assumptions: -55 mV is a reasonable approximation of the in vivo IHC resting potential
Capacitance measurements at -55 mV are technically valid despite the different baseline conditions
evaluation.notes: This is one of the most compelling demonstrations in the paper, directly linking recording conditions to physiological relevance. The progressive worsening across holding potentials strongly supports the in vivo significance of the phenotype.

nodes.label: This exocytosis phenotype was observed neither in Cabp1 nor in Cabp2 single KO a…
nodes.claim: This exocytosis phenotype was observed neither in Cabp1 nor in Cabp2 single KO animals, indicating the combined loss reveals a synergistic deficit.
nodes.verbatim_quote: Such phenotype was observed neither in Cabp1 nor in Cabp2 single KO animals

strengths: Direct comparison to previously published single KO data (Picher, 2017; Yang et al., 2018)
The emergence of a dramatic exocytosis phenotype only in the DKO strongly supports synergistic/redundant function
Consistent with the electrophysiological data showing more pronounced CaV1.3 inactivation in DKO vs single KOs
weaknesses: Comparisons to single KO exocytosis data are from different studies with potentially different experimental conditions
Single KO exocytosis measurements were performed at -85 mV, which may mask a phenotype that becomes apparent at more depolarized holding potentials (as shown for the DKO)
It is not clear whether single KO animals were tested at elevated holding potentials
alternative_interpretations: The single KO phenotype might have been detected if tested at -55 mV holding potential, potentially narrowing the perceived gap between single KO and DKO
required_assumptions: Recording conditions were sufficiently comparable across studies
The absence of a phenotype in single KOs at -85 mV genuinely reflects compensatory mechanisms rather than insufficient sensitivity
evaluation.notes: This is a key claim for the paper's central thesis. The logic is sound but would be strengthened by testing single KOs at elevated holding potentials.

nodes.label: ABR thresholds are severely elevated in young DKO animals with tone bursts up to…
nodes.claim: ABR thresholds are severely elevated in young DKO animals with tone bursts up to 90 dB SPL barely eliciting responses, and click thresholds are approximately 30 dB higher than WT, with progressive worsening by 7–13 weeks.
nodes.verbatim_quote: Already in young (3- to 4-week-old) Cabp1/2-DKO animals, ABR thresholds were highly elevated, with tone bursts up to a maximum intensity of 90 dB SPL barely eliciting any ABR response.

strengths: Clear ABR data with large threshold elevations: tone bursts barely eliciting responses at 90 dB, clicks at 59 vs 30 dB SPL
Progressive worsening documented: click thresholds 68 dB at 7-13 weeks vs 59 dB at 3-4 weeks
Adequate sample sizes (N = 8-9 per genotype for young, N = 7 for older)
Sub-claim c1.3.1.1 rated strong/calibrated
weaknesses: Tone burst thresholds assigned 100 dB when exceeding 90 dB maximum, which is a ceiling artifact
Age groups somewhat broad (particularly 7-13 weeks)
Progressive worsening could include contributions beyond CaV1.3 inactivation (e.g., hair cell degeneration)
alternative_interpretations: The progressive component could reflect cumulative excitotoxic or degenerative changes rather than solely progressive CaV1.3 inactivation
required_assumptions: ABR threshold measurements are performed consistently across genotypes and ages
The ceiling assignment of 100 dB does not significantly bias the analysis
evaluation.notes: The ABR data is unambiguous in demonstrating severe hearing loss. The ceiling artifact is minor given the overall magnitude of threshold elevation.

nodes.label: Spiral ganglion neuron responses in vivo are extremely scarce, with drastically …
nodes.claim: Spiral ganglion neuron responses in vivo are extremely scarce, with drastically reduced peak and adapted spike rates, increased first-spike latency and jitter, and greatly enhanced adaptation strength.
nodes.verbatim_quote: Single neuron responses to sound stimulation in vivo in the region of the auditory nerve of Cabp1/2-DKO mice were extremely scarce.

strengths: In vivo single-unit recordings provide direct evidence of SGN dysfunction
Multiple quantitative metrics reported: peak/adapted rates, latency (12.5 vs 4.8 ms, p < 0.001), jitter (18.3 vs 1.5, p < 0.00001), adaptation strength (peak/adapted ratio 12.5 vs 3.4, p < 0.00001)
Systematic manipulation of stimulus repetition rate reveals rate-dependent recovery
Multiple sub-claims (c1.3.2.1-c1.3.2.4) provide converging evidence
weaknesses: Severe selection bias: only 0.3 vs 2.5 neurons/hour recording yield; detected neurons likely overrepresent less-affected units (acknowledged by authors)
Only 1/20 DKO neurons showed normal tuning—inability to determine characteristic frequency in most units means stimulation was suboptimal
3/19 DKO units may be cochlear nucleus neurons rather than SGNs, introducing classification uncertainty
The low yield (sub-claim c1.3.2.4, rated moderate) is an observational metric that could be influenced by factors beyond neural activity
alternative_interpretations: Some detected 'SGN' responses could be from cochlear nucleus neurons, inflating apparent SGN responsiveness
The enhanced adaptation could partly reflect post-synaptic mechanisms (e.g., SGN membrane property changes) rather than purely presynaptic
required_assumptions: Unit classification based on location, response patterns, and spike waveforms is reliable
The selection bias does not invalidate the qualitative conclusions about impaired sound encoding
The use of broadband noise or subjective best frequency stimulation provides adequate stimulation for characterization
evaluation.notes: Despite the selection bias, the data strongly supports severely impaired sound encoding. The authors appropriately acknowledge the limitations. The rate-dependence of recovery (Figure 7D) is particularly informative.

nodes.label: Cochlear amplification by outer hair cells is largely preserved in DKO animals, …
nodes.claim: Cochlear amplification by outer hair cells is largely preserved in DKO animals, indicating the hearing impairment is primarily of IHC synaptic origin.
nodes.verbatim_quote: Our results suggest that cochlear amplification is largely preserved also in DKO animals

strengths: DPOAEs measured systematically across frequencies
Normal DPOAEs in ~50% of animals at both ages tested
Consistent with prior work showing preserved cochlear amplification in Cabp2 single KO (Yang et al., 2018; Picher, 2017)
weaknesses: Approximately half of DKO animals showed reduced DPOAE amplitudes, weakening the 'largely preserved' qualifier
Different setups with different calibrations used for the two age groups, limiting direct comparison
Significant increase in DPOAE thresholds at 7-13 weeks (p < 0.002, two-way ANOVA)
Sub-claim c1.3.3.1 rated moderate/calibrated
alternative_interpretations: Reduced DPOAEs in half of animals could indicate emerging OHC dysfunction or secondary pathology
Middle ear pathology from surgical manipulation could contribute to reduced DPOAEs in some animals
required_assumptions: DPOAEs faithfully report OHC function
The variation between animals reflects biological variability rather than technical factors
evaluation.notes: The qualifier 'largely preserved' is appropriate given the data, but the claim would be more accurate as 'partially preserved' given that ~50% of animals show reduced DPOAEs. The authors use appropriate hedging.

nodes.label: ABR wave I is absent or greatly reduced while later ABR peaks are better preserv…
nodes.claim: ABR wave I is absent or greatly reduced while later ABR peaks are better preserved, suggesting reduced and/or desynchronized SGN spiking rather than a brainstem defect.
nodes.verbatim_quote: Upon 80 dB SPL click stimulation, no sizable ABR wave I was detected in average traces of DKO animals...the later ABR peaks were better preserved, indicating partially preserved activation of neurons of the auditory brainstem.

strengths: Clear ABR waveform analysis showing absent/reduced wave I with better-preserved later peaks
Average waveform traces at 80 dB SPL demonstrate the pattern clearly
Interpretation is consistent with the known generator sources of ABR waves
Pattern is consistent with other IHC synapse mutants (Khimich et al., 2005; Strenzke et al., 2016)
weaknesses: Average traces may mask individual variability
Later waves being 'better preserved' is relative—they may still be significantly reduced
The pattern could also be consistent with desynchronization at the first synapse rather than reduced output per se
alternative_interpretations: Better preservation of later waves could reflect central gain compensation rather than purely preserved brainstem function
required_assumptions: ABR wave I amplitude reflects SGN synchronous firing
Later waves reflect brainstem processing of the residual input
evaluation.notes: This is a well-established pattern in IHC synaptopathies and supports the synaptic origin interpretation.

nodes.label: Pre- and postsynaptic immunofluorescence intensities are increased in DKO IHCs, …
nodes.claim: Pre- and postsynaptic immunofluorescence intensities are increased in DKO IHCs, consistent with compensatory synaptic changes in conditions of very little postsynaptic activity.
nodes.verbatim_quote: the intensities of pre- (RibeyeA/CtBP2) and postsynaptic (Homer1) immunofluorescent puncta were increased in the CaBP1/2-deficient IHCs

strengths: Quantitative analysis of immunofluorescence intensity from large numbers of puncta (614 and 441 from WT and DKO)
Both pre- (RibeyeA/CtBP2) and postsynaptic (Homer1) markers increased
Parallel processing of WT and DKO samples reduces batch effects
Statistical significance (Wilcoxon rank-sum test, p < 0.005)
Consistent with changes seen in other synaptic mutants (Eckrich et al., 2019; Kim et al., 2019)
weaknesses: Immunofluorescence intensity is semi-quantitative and influenced by tissue processing, antibody penetration, and imaging parameters
Interpretation as 'compensatory changes' is speculative—increased protein could reflect reduced turnover, altered transcription, or other mechanisms
Not observed in Cabp2 single KO, suggesting this requires a threshold level of dysfunction
alternative_interpretations: Increased immunofluorescence could reflect protein accumulation due to reduced exocytosis/endocytosis rather than compensatory upregulation
Changes could be developmental rather than compensatory
required_assumptions: Immunofluorescence intensity correlates with protein abundance
Parallel processing adequately controls for technical variability
evaluation.notes: The interpretation as 'compensatory postsynaptic changes' is reasonable but speculative. The data itself is robust.

nodes.label: BK channel clusters at IHC necks are significantly smaller and fewer in DKO IHCs…
nodes.claim: BK channel clusters at IHC necks are significantly smaller and fewer in DKO IHCs, suggesting downstream effects on BK channel expression.
nodes.verbatim_quote: the BK channel clusters appeared smaller in the DKO IHCs as compared to controls

strengths: Quantitative analysis using Imaris software for BK-cluster volume measurements
Statistical significance (p < 0.0001, N = 6 organs per genotype)
Both individual cluster volume and cumulative BK volume per IHC measured (14.2 vs 6.6 µm³, p < 0.01)
Partial reversal by CaBP2 expression supports CaBP-dependence
Progressive worsening at 14 weeks compared to 3-4 weeks
weaknesses: Immunofluorescence 'volume' is a proxy for protein abundance, not a direct measure (inherited from sub-claim c1.3.6.1)
The mechanism linking CaBP1/2 loss to BK channel reduction is entirely speculative
Authors acknowledge this could be direct (transcription factor role) or indirect (impaired Ca2+ signaling), neither of which is tested
alternative_interpretations: Reduced BK expression could be a secondary consequence of altered IHC Ca2+ homeostasis rather than a direct CaBP effect
Changes could reflect accelerated aging/degeneration of IHCs in the DKO
required_assumptions: Immunofluorescence volume correlates with functional BK channel density
The BK phenotype is mechanistically related to CaBP absence rather than being an epiphenomenon
evaluation.notes: The observation is well-documented but the mechanistic interpretation remains open. The authors appropriately note this needs future testing.

nodes.label: IHC maturation markers indicate largely normal developmental transition in DKO a…
nodes.claim: IHC maturation markers indicate largely normal developmental transition in DKO animals, with SK2 mostly absent by 3 weeks and BK channels transitioning to neck patches, though BK clusters become progressively smaller.
nodes.verbatim_quote: As expected for normal maturation, the SK2 puncta were mostly absent from DKO IHCs by 3 weeks of age and the BK puncta underwent a typical transition from a spotty appearance throughout the cell membrane to the patches at the IHC necks

strengths: SK2 absence by 3 weeks and BK transition to neck patches observed, consistent with normal maturation timeline
Direct comparison with immature (1-week-old) cochleae confirms developmental trajectory
Progressive BK cluster size reduction documented across ages
weaknesses: Occasional SK2 immunofluorescent spots still detected in 3-week-old DKO IHCs, though authors note this also occurs rarely in WT
BK cluster reduction represents an abnormality within the context of otherwise normal developmental markers
Functional implications of smaller BK clusters are not directly tested
alternative_interpretations: The presence of rare SK2 spots could indicate subtly delayed maturation in a subset of IHCs
Normal maturation of some markers does not rule out delayed maturation of other unexamined markers
required_assumptions: SK2 downregulation and BK localization transition are reliable markers of IHC maturation
3-week time point is sufficient to confirm completed maturation
evaluation.notes: The normal developmental transition is important as it distinguishes this phenotype from CaV1.3 channelopathies where maturation is arrested (Brandt et al., 2003; Neef et al., 2009). The BK cluster size reduction adds nuance but does not invalidate the overall maturation conclusion.

nodes.label: Isolated disruption of CaBP1 in mice leaves hearing unperturbed for the first fe…
nodes.claim: Isolated disruption of CaBP1 in mice leaves hearing unperturbed for the first few months, and isolated disruption of CaBP2 causes only moderate progressive hearing impairment, while the DKO causes immediate severe impairment.
nodes.verbatim_quote: isolated disruption of CaBP1 or CaBP4 in mice leads to at most modest enhancement of IHC CaV1.3 inactivation

strengths: Relies on well-established published data from Yang et al., 2018 (Cabp1 KO) and Picher, 2017 (Cabp2 KO)
The dramatic severity of DKO phenotype relative to single KOs is directly demonstrated in the current study
Consistent narrative across ABR, patch-clamp, and single-unit data
weaknesses: No new expression data generated in this study; relies entirely on previously published work for the single KO characterization (inherited from sub-claim c1.4.1.1, rated moderate)
Characterization of CaBP2 KO as causing 'only moderate progressive hearing impairment' may understate its severity—the phenotype is progressive and becomes severe
Direct side-by-side comparison of all three genotypes (Cabp1 KO, Cabp2 KO, DKO) under identical conditions was not performed for all measurements
alternative_interpretations: The DKO phenotype could be more than additive (synergistic) rather than simply revealing the combined contribution, suggesting additional downstream effects of losing both CaBPs simultaneously
required_assumptions: Prior single KO characterizations are accurate and relevant to the current study
The C57/Bl6 background is comparable across studies
Age-matched comparisons are valid despite different study timelines
evaluation.notes: The claim accurately summarizes the literature but the inference of 'immediate severe impairment' in DKO is well-supported by the current study's ABR data.

nodes.label: The inability of CaBP1 to fully replace CaBP2 in CaBP2-deficient IHCs may stem f…
nodes.claim: The inability of CaBP1 to fully replace CaBP2 in CaBP2-deficient IHCs may stem from either insufficient CaBP1 concentration or from distinct properties of the two proteins.
nodes.verbatim_quote: The inability of CaBP1 to fully replace CaBP2 in the CaBP2-deficient IHCs may stem from either too low concentration of CaBP1 (and other CaBPs), or from distinct properties of the two proteins

strengths: Logically sound inference from the observation that CaBP1 only partially compensates for CaBP2 loss
Two explanations offered (concentration vs. distinct properties) are both plausible
Supported by published expression data suggesting lower CaBP1 than CaBP2 levels in IHCs (Yang et al., 2016)
weaknesses: Entirely speculative—no experiments distinguish between concentration and distinct-properties explanations
No CaBP1 overexpression experiments performed to test the concentration hypothesis
No biochemical comparison of CaBP1 vs CaBP2 interaction with IHC CaV1.3 channels presented
alternative_interpretations: CaBP1 and CaBP2 may target different subsets of CaV1.3 channels at the synapse rather than having overlapping but differential potency
Subcellular localization differences could be the key factor rather than concentration or biochemical properties
required_assumptions: CaBP1 and CaBP2 compete for the same binding sites on CaV1.3 channels
The relevant comparison is between CaBP1 and CaBP2 at the IHC ribbon synapse specifically
evaluation.notes: This is a discussion-level interpretation appropriately framed as hypothesis. The authors correctly note that future experiments involving CaBP1 overexpression and chimeric constructs are needed.

nodes.label: The hearing impairment of the DKO is interpreted as primarily due to defects of …
nodes.claim: The hearing impairment of the DKO is interpreted as primarily due to defects of hair cell function, with SGN dysfunction judged as rather unlikely, because Cabp1 KO animals show normal hearing at early ages and CaBP2 is absent from SGNs.
nodes.verbatim_quote: Since Cabp1 KO animals show normal hearing several weeks after birth, and CaBP2 is absent from SGNs, we interpret the hearing impairment of the Cabp1/2 DKO animals to be primarily due to defects of hair cell function

strengths: Logical argument: Cabp1 KO hearing is normal early, and CaBP2 appears absent from SGNs (Yang et al., 2016)
The IHC-specific phenotype (CaV1.3 inactivation, exocytosis deficits) directly explains hearing loss
Gene rescue targeting IHCs (via PHP.eB-Cabp2) partially restores hearing, supporting IHC-centric causality
weaknesses: CaBP1 expression includes caldendrin in SGNs/glia—its loss could affect SGN function independently, which is not tested
Inference that SGN dysfunction is 'rather unlikely' may be too strong given that caldendrin is present in SGNs and its function there is unknown
The PHP.eB vector may also transduce SGNs (eGFP detected 'elsewhere'), potentially confounding the rescue interpretation
Inferential gap: the premises (Cabp1 KO normal hearing; CaBP2 absent from SGNs) individually do not exclude SGN contributions in the DKO context where both are absent simultaneously
alternative_interpretations: Loss of caldendrin in SGNs could contribute to the more severe DKO phenotype through post-synaptic mechanisms
CaBP1 might have a modulatory role in SGN that is only unmasked when combined with CaBP2 loss in IHCs
required_assumptions: CaBP2 is truly absent from SGNs (based on expression data)
Normal early hearing in Cabp1 KO implies CaBP1 is not essential for SGN function in the first weeks
Viral rescue targeting IHCs validates the IHC-centric interpretation
evaluation.notes: The interpretation is reasonable as a primary hypothesis but the 'rather unlikely' qualifier for SGN contribution may be slightly overclaimed given the presence of caldendrin in SGNs.

nodes.label: Transgenic expression of CaBP2 partially restores the 'non-inactivating' nature …
nodes.claim: Transgenic expression of CaBP2 partially restores the 'non-inactivating' nature of IHC CaV1.3 channels in DKO animals.
nodes.verbatim_quote: The 'non-inactivating' nature of the IHC CaV1.3 channels was partially restored in the Cabp1/2-DKOs by transgenic expression of WT CaBP2 (Student's t-test: p < 0.0001)

strengths: Clear statistical significance (p < 0.0001) for rescue of inactivation fraction
Demonstrated across multiple stimulus paradigms (500-ms step and train stimuli)
Consistent with prior work showing CaBP2 suppresses CaV1.3 inactivation in HEK cells and single KO IHCs (Picher, 2017; Oestreicher et al., 2021)
Sub-claim c1.5.1.1 rated strong/calibrated
weaknesses: Rescue is incomplete ('partial restoration'), leaving open whether this reflects insufficient expression or irreversible changes
Train stimulus data from cells with lower-than-average inactivation (0.36 vs 0.47), potentially biasing rescue assessment for this measure (inherited from sub-claim c1.5.1.1)
The voltage shift was not rescued, suggesting some changes are CaBP2-independent or irreversible
L-isoform used for rescue may not be the predominant IHC isoform (CaBP2-alt may be more abundant)
alternative_interpretations: Incomplete rescue could indicate that CaBP1 has unique functions not replaceable by CaBP2
The wrong splice isoform (L vs. alt) could limit rescue efficacy
required_assumptions: PHP.eB-mediated CaBP2 expression reaches relevant sites within IHCs
The L-isoform of CaBP2 is functionally relevant for CaV1.3 modulation in IHCs
evaluation.notes: The rescue is convincing but the incomplete nature is noted. The use of the L-isoform rather than the potentially more abundant CaBP2-alt isoform is a limitation the authors acknowledge in the discussion.

nodes.label: CaBP2 transgenic expression largely restored the efficiency of exocytosis in DKO…
nodes.claim: CaBP2 transgenic expression largely restored the efficiency of exocytosis in DKO IHCs, including at elevated holding potentials.
nodes.verbatim_quote: Transgenic expression of CaBP2 largely restored the efficiency of exocytosis, indicating that the impairment as observed in the IHCs of DKOs is related to the absence of the CaBPs.

strengths: Exocytosis efficiency (ΔCm/QCa) significantly rescued by CaBP2 expression
Rescue demonstrated at both -85 mV (p < 0.01 for 100-200 ms) and -55 mV holding potentials (p < 0.05)
Consistent with partial rescue of Ca2+ currents and QCa
Functional rescue at elevated holding potential is particularly convincing for physiological relevance
weaknesses: Efficiency rescue at long pulse durations could be confounded by altered endocytosis rates in transduced cells
The rescued cells may represent a biased sample of successfully transduced IHCs with adequate CaBP2 expression
The non-rescued exocytosis phenotype is partly attributed to unknown mechanisms beyond Ca2+ influx—whether these are also rescued by CaBP2 is not clear
alternative_interpretations: Improved exocytosis efficiency could partly reflect better vesicle replenishment due to restored Ca2+-dependent priming rather than purely more Ca2+ entry
required_assumptions: Transduced IHCs are representative
CaBP2 expression levels are sufficient for meaningful rescue
Efficiency metric is valid across conditions
evaluation.notes: The rescue of exocytosis efficiency, not just total exocytosis, is an important finding suggesting CaBPs may have roles beyond simply maintaining Ca2+ influx.

nodes.label: ABR thresholds are significantly improved, click-evoked ABR amplitudes increased…
nodes.claim: ABR thresholds are significantly improved, click-evoked ABR amplitudes increased, and wave I latency shortened upon CaBP2 transgenic expression in DKO animals.
nodes.verbatim_quote: Transgenic expression of CaBP2 in DKO animals led to significantly improved hearing with lower ABR thresholds, increased click-evoked ABR amplitudes, and shortened wave I latency

strengths: Significant ABR threshold improvements across all tested frequencies and click stimuli (Table in Supplementary file 1)
Increased ABR wave I amplitude at 80 dB (p ≤ 0.0001)
Shortened wave I latency
Strong eGFP immunofluorescence confirming successful transduction along the cochlear length
Sub-claim c1.5.3.1 rated strong/calibrated
weaknesses: Thresholds did not completely recover to WT levels (inherited from sub-claim c1.5.3.1)
Lower eGFP expression toward the cochlear base may correlate with incomplete high-frequency rescue
Unilateral injection design means contralateral ear effects (some eGFP detected) may confound ABR measurements
No contralateral ear ABR data presented for comparison
alternative_interpretations: Some hearing improvement could be due to CaBP2 expression in cell types other than IHCs (e.g., if transduction also affects SGNs or OHCs)
The strong eGFP signal 'elsewhere' in the cochlea raises questions about off-target effects
required_assumptions: ABR improvements reflect IHC-specific rescue rather than other transduced cell types
Unilateral recording accurately captures ipsilateral rescue effects
The PHP.eB vector preferentially targets IHCs for CaBP2 expression
evaluation.notes: The in vivo hearing rescue is the strongest translational finding of the paper. The incomplete rescue is honestly discussed.

nodes.label: The rescue is incomplete: tone burst and click thresholds did not fully recover …
nodes.claim: The rescue is incomplete: tone burst and click thresholds did not fully recover to WT levels, possibly due to inadequate expression levels, irreversible adaptive changes, or distinct requirements for CaBPs at different synapse types.
nodes.verbatim_quote: The lack of complete recovery suggests either an inadequate expression of transgenic material or irreversible adaptive changes in response to the lack of major CaBPs that may occur prior to gene delivery.

strengths: Multiple plausible explanations offered for incomplete rescue
Authors explicitly distinguish between threshold and suprathreshold recovery
Discussion of possible roles for different CaBPs at different synapse types is biologically sophisticated
Honest assessment of limitations
weaknesses: Multiple non-exclusive explanations offered without ability to distinguish between them
No experiments directly testing any of the proposed explanations (inadequate expression, irreversible changes, synapse-type specificity)
The use of the L-isoform rather than the alt isoform is not explicitly tested as a possible factor
Possible adverse effects of overexpression are mentioned but not systematically investigated
alternative_interpretations: Timing of viral delivery may be too late if critical developmental windows have passed
The promoter (hCMV/HBA) may not drive expression patterns matching endogenous CaBP2 spatially or temporally
required_assumptions: Complete rescue is in principle achievable with optimal expression conditions
The incomplete rescue reflects biological limitations rather than technical failures
evaluation.notes: This is largely a discussion claim. The speculation is appropriate and well-hedged, but no experiments address the specific reasons for incomplete rescue.

nodes.label: Suprathreshold ABR wave I responses were very large in CaBP2-rescued DKO animals…
nodes.claim: Suprathreshold ABR wave I responses were very large in CaBP2-rescued DKO animals, and summated wave I–IV responses were not distinguishable from WT, despite incomplete threshold recovery.
nodes.verbatim_quote: suprathreshold responses of ABR wave I were very large...and the summated wave I–IV responses were not distinguishable from WT responses

strengths: Clear quantitative demonstration of large suprathreshold wave I amplitudes in rescued animals
Summated wave I-IV analysis (Figure 6—figure supplement 2C) provides robust comparison with WT
Statistical significance reported (Tukey's multicomparison test, p < 0.0001 for DKO vs WT or vs injected DKO)
The dissociation between threshold and suprathreshold recovery is an interesting and well-documented finding
weaknesses: Very large wave I in rescued animals could reflect overexpression-driven enhancement beyond normal levels
No single KO comparison for suprathreshold responses to assess whether CaBP1 absence contributes to the large wave I (as suggested for young Cabp1 KOs)
The discrepancy between threshold and suprathreshold rescue is intriguing but not mechanistically explained
alternative_interpretations: Large suprathreshold wave I could reflect overexpression-driven hypersynchronization of SGN firing
Combined CaBP2 overexpression with CaBP1 absence might produce an additive 'gain-of-function' effect at suprathreshold levels
required_assumptions: ABR wave amplitudes faithfully reflect SGN population synchrony and firing rates
The comparison with WT is valid despite different genetic backgrounds and potential overexpression
evaluation.notes: The dissociation between threshold recovery (incomplete) and suprathreshold response (full or even enhanced) is one of the most interesting findings and merits further investigation. The authors' speculation about different CaBP requirements at synapses providing inputs to different SGN fiber types is creative but untested.

nodes.label: Recovery from inactivation after prolonged mild stimulation (2-min sine wave) is…
nodes.claim: Recovery from inactivation after prolonged mild stimulation (2-min sine wave) is slowed in DKO IHCs, requiring a double exponential fit with a slow component, unlike the single exponential in WT.
nodes.verbatim_quote: in the absence of CaBP1 and 2 even mild but prolonged stimulation of IHCs in vivo may drive a significant fraction of CaV1.3 channels into 'deep-state' of inactivation with very slow recovery

strengths: Systematic recovery protocol with defined conditioning stimuli (500-ms step vs 2-min sine wave)
Clear difference in recovery kinetics between WT (single exponential) and DKO (double exponential required) after sine wave
Partial rescue by CaBP2 expression (smaller and faster slow component)
Table 1 provides quantitative fit parameters
Sub-claim c1.6.1.1 rated strong/calibrated
weaknesses: Sample sizes for recovery experiments not stated in text excerpt
The 2-min sine wave is a reasonable but imperfect proxy for sustained in vivo stimulation
The concept of 'deep-state inactivation' is borrowed from NaV/KV literature and may not directly apply to CaV1.3 channels
No direct evidence that the slow recovery component reflects a specific biophysical state rather than, e.g., altered Ca2+ homeostasis
alternative_interpretations: The slow recovery component could reflect impaired Ca2+ extrusion or buffering in DKO IHCs rather than channel-intrinsic slow inactivation
Post-translational modifications accumulating during prolonged stimulation could slow recovery independently of CaBP function
required_assumptions: The sine wave conditioning stimulus adequately mimics physiological stimulation
The recovery kinetics primarily reflect CaV1.3 channel state transitions
Single vs double exponential fitting accurately captures the underlying biophysics
evaluation.notes: This is a well-designed experiment that provides important mechanistic insight. The distinction between responses to brief intense vs. prolonged mild stimulation is particularly valuable for understanding in vivo relevance.

nodes.label: Recovery from a 500-ms depolarization was paradoxically faster in DKO than in WT…
nodes.claim: Recovery from a 500-ms depolarization was paradoxically faster in DKO than in WT or CaBP2-rescued IHCs, which the authors attribute to faster Ca2+ clearance due to less Ca2+ entry from pronounced inactivation.
nodes.verbatim_quote: the speed of recovery from inactivation was fast both in DKO as well as WT IHCs...However, the recovery from the step-evoked inactivation was slowest in the Cabp2-injected DKO IHCs.

strengths: Data clearly shows faster recovery in DKO than WT/rescued IHCs after 500-ms depolarization
Specific quantitative values provided: time constants 0.62 s (DKO) vs 0.75 s (WT)
Initial inactivation fraction quantified: I10ms_post/Ipre WT 0.73, DKO 0.36, rescued 0.64
Authors provide a thoughtful mechanistic hypothesis
weaknesses: The Ca2+ clearance hypothesis is entirely speculative—no Ca2+ imaging was performed (acknowledged by authors as needed for future work)
The paradoxical finding complicates straightforward interpretation of CaBP function (inherited from sub-claim c1.6.2.1)
Alternative hypothesis about CaBP2 as slow mobile buffer is presented but not tested
The fastest recovery in DKO could also reflect qualitatively different inactivation states (primarily VDI) with inherently faster recovery
The slowest recovery in rescued DKO raises concerns about potential artifacts of CaBP2 overexpression
alternative_interpretations: DKO channels may primarily undergo VDI (which recovers faster) while rescued channels with CaBP2 have more CDI (which may recover slower due to Ca2+-dependent processes)
Overexpressed CaBP2 acting as a Ca2+ buffer could prolong Ca2+ transients and CDI, explaining the slow recovery
The 500-ms recovery may primarily report Ca2+ clearance kinetics rather than channel-intrinsic properties
required_assumptions: Recovery kinetics reflect a combination of channel state transitions and Ca2+ clearance
Less Ca2+ entry in DKO leads to faster Ca2+ clearance and thus faster CDI recovery
The comparison between 500-ms pulse and sine wave recovery reveals different inactivation states
evaluation.notes: This finding is genuinely interesting and the authors' interpretation is plausible, but the lack of supporting Ca2+ imaging data limits the mechanistic conclusions. The claim is appropriately hedged with 'we hypothesize.'

nodes.label: The activity-dependent worsening of the synaptic phenotype is demonstrated by th…
nodes.claim: The activity-dependent worsening of the synaptic phenotype is demonstrated by the pronounced deterioration of exocytosis with higher holding potentials and larger sine wave amplitudes during recordings.
nodes.verbatim_quote: We thus reduced the sine wave amplitude, which resulted in an intermediate phenotype, indicating pronounced activity-dependent deterioration of synaptic function in the absence of CaBPs

strengths: Systematic manipulation of three variables: holding potential (-85, -65, -55 mV), sine wave amplitude, and stimulus duration
Progressive worsening demonstrated across conditions (Figure 3D, E)
Intermediate phenotype with reduced sine wave amplitude provides elegant internal control
60% vs 25% Ca2+ current reduction at -55 mV in DKO vs WT quantifies the differential effect
Consistent with the in vivo SGN data showing rate-dependent deterioration
weaknesses: The exact contribution of sine wave-induced channel activation is difficult to quantify precisely
The 'activity-dependent deterioration' could partly reflect rundown of patched cells, though this would affect both genotypes
In vivo conditions involve much more complex temporal patterns of stimulation than simple sine waves
alternative_interpretations: Progressive deterioration could partially reflect accumulation of recording-induced artifacts at more depolarized potentials
The sine wave effect could reflect Ca2+-dependent processes beyond channel inactivation (e.g., Ca2+-dependent endocytosis affecting capacitance measurements)
required_assumptions: Sine wave and elevated holding potential conditions reasonably approximate physiological IHC activity
The progressive worsening is specific to CaBP absence and not a general property of patched IHCs at depolarized potentials
evaluation.notes: This is one of the strongest experimental contributions of the paper. The demonstration that recording conditions dramatically affect phenotype severity has important implications for interpreting prior single KO results and for understanding in vivo pathophysiology.

nodes.label: VDI was 0.30 ± 0.02 in DKO vs 0.13 ± 0.02 in WT IHCs, and CDI was 0.65 ± 0.01 in…
nodes.claim: VDI was 0.30 ± 0.02 in DKO vs 0.13 ± 0.02 in WT IHCs, and CDI was 0.65 ± 0.01 in DKO vs 0.11 ± 0.02 in WT IHCs (p < 0.0001).
