nodes.verbatim_quote: VDI: 0.30 ± 0.02 vs 0.13 ± 0.02 and CDI: 0.65 ± 0.01 vs 0.11 ± 0.02 in Cabp1/2 DKO and WT IHCs, respectively; p < 0.0001, Student's t-test

strengths: Clear quantitative data with small SEMs for both VDI and CDI measurements
Appropriate use of Ba2+ substitution to dissect VDI from CDI, following established methodology (Tadross et al., 2010)
Highly significant p-values (p < 0.0001) for both measures
Methodological approach of separating VDI and CDI is well-established in the CaV channel literature
The CDI enhancement (~6-fold) in DKO is much larger than VDI enhancement (~2-fold), consistent with CaBPs primarily opposing CaM-mediated CDI
weaknesses: Sample sizes (n values) for these specific measurements are not explicitly stated in the text excerpt for the 2 mM condition (though n=13 for 2 mM DKO condition is mentioned in supplement description)
Recordings were performed at room temperature with 2 mM extracellular Ca2+, which may not reflect physiological conditions
Only Student's t-test was used; given the large effect sizes this is unlikely problematic, but reporting of normality assumptions is absent
alternative_interpretations: Enhanced inactivation could partly reflect altered CaV1.3 splice variant expression or auxiliary subunit composition in DKO, not solely loss of direct CaBP modulation
required_assumptions: Ba2+ adequately substitutes for Ca2+ in assessing VDI without introducing artifacts
The mathematical separation of VDI and CDI using the Tadross method is valid for IHC CaV1.3 channels
evaluation.notes: These values are central to the paper's main thesis. The effect sizes are very large, making them robust to moderate methodological concerns.

nodes.label: Half-activation potential V0.5 was –33.6 ± 0.5 mV in DKO vs –30.9 ± 0.5 mV in WT…
nodes.claim: Half-activation potential V0.5 was –33.6 ± 0.5 mV in DKO vs –30.9 ± 0.5 mV in WT (p < 0.0001), and activation slope was 7.6 ± 0.1 vs 7.1 ± 0.1 (p < 0.0001).
nodes.verbatim_quote: V0.5 of –33.6 ± 0.5 to –30.9 ± 0.5 mV in Cabp1/2 DKO and WT IHCs, respectively; p < 0.0001

strengths: Precise quantitative measurements with tight SEMs
Highly significant p-values for both V0.5 and slope
The authors explicitly acknowledge the unexpected direction of the V0.5 shift (hyperpolarized rather than depolarized), demonstrating intellectual honesty
weaknesses: The hyperpolarized shift is opposite to what heterologous expression systems predict, and the authors acknowledge they cannot currently explain this discrepancy
Authors suggest possible confounds from splice variant changes or auxiliary subunit alterations, which are unresolved
The shift (~2.7 mV) and slope difference (~0.5) are small in absolute terms, and their physiological significance is uncertain
alternative_interpretations: Compensatory changes in CaV1.3 splice variant expression or auxiliary subunit composition could drive the V0.5 shift independently of CaBP loss
The opposite direction from heterologous expression predictions could indicate that in native IHCs, CaBPs are not the primary determinants of activation voltage
required_assumptions: Boltzmann fits adequately describe the activation curves
Leak subtraction and liquid junction potential corrections are accurate
evaluation.notes: The authors handle this unexpected finding transparently, noting it contradicts heterologous expression data (Haeseleer et al., 2004; Picher, 2017; Shaltiel et al., 2012). This honesty is commendable but the finding remains unexplained.

nodes.label: Ribbon synapse counts were comparable: 12.9 ± 0.2 in WT vs 12.8 ± 0.8 in DKO at …
nodes.claim: Ribbon synapse counts were comparable: 12.9 ± 0.2 in WT vs 12.8 ± 0.8 in DKO at 3 weeks of age.
nodes.verbatim_quote: comparable abundance of ribbon synapses in the apical IHCs of WT and DKO animals (12.9 ± 0.2 vs 12.8 ± 0.8, respectively)

strengths: Direct quantitative comparison with very similar numbers (12.9 vs 12.8)
Consistent with the notion that CaBP1/2 loss does not affect synaptogenesis
Immunolabeling with established pre- and postsynaptic markers (RibeyeA/CtBP2, Homer1)
weaknesses: Only assessed at 3 weeks of age; later time points may differ
N (number of animals or organs) for this specific count is not explicitly stated in the excerpt
The SEM for DKO (0.8) is notably larger than for WT (0.2), suggesting more variability in DKO
alternative_interpretations: Normal synapse number does not exclude functional differences at individual synapses
required_assumptions: Immunolabeling accurately identifies all ribbon synapses
The tonotopic position examined is representative
evaluation.notes: This negative finding is important for interpretation—it rules out synapse loss as a confound for the functional phenotype.

nodes.label: Significant impairment of sustained exocytosis at –85 mV (p < 0.05 for 20 ms, p …
nodes.claim: Significant impairment of sustained exocytosis at –85 mV (p < 0.05 for 20 ms, p < 0.001 for 100- and 200-ms steps) and reduced QCa (p < 0.005 for longest pulses) compared to WT.
nodes.verbatim_quote: CaBP1/2-deficient inner hair cells (IHCs) showed significant impairment of the sustained exocytosis (p < 0.05 for 20 ms, and <0.001 for 100- and 200-ms step, respectively)

strengths: Multiple pulse durations tested systematically (2–200 ms), allowing RRP vs sustained exocytosis dissection
Both ΔCm and QCa are reported, enabling assessment of exocytosis efficiency
Statistical significance achieved across multiple time points
Appropriate use of unpaired t-tests with Welch correction
weaknesses: Sample sizes for individual pulse durations are not explicitly stated in this excerpt
Recordings at –85 mV holding potential may underestimate the in vivo phenotype severity, as the authors themselves later demonstrate
alternative_interpretations: Reduced QCa alone could explain part of the exocytosis deficit without invoking additional mechanisms
Endocytic changes could contribute to ΔCm measurements, complicating interpretation of exocytosis
required_assumptions: ΔCm faithfully reports exocytosis
Perforated patch configuration preserves intracellular milieu sufficiently
evaluation.notes: The authors appropriately note that the exocytosis deficit exceeds what can be explained by reduced QCa, and this is further explored in Figure 3C.

nodes.label: CaBPs may directly affect exocytosis beyond calcium channel modulation, potentia…
nodes.claim: CaBPs may directly affect exocytosis beyond calcium channel modulation, potentially through CaMKII modulation influencing otoferlin Ca2+ affinity, or through other mechanisms involving synaptic protein interactions.
nodes.verbatim_quote: it is worth noting that CaBP1 and 2 have been reported to modulate CaMKII activity...which in turn may through phosphorylation modify the Ca2+ affinity of otoferlin C2 domains

strengths: The authors appropriately frame this as speculative ('it is worth noting', 'may', 'need to be tested')
The suggestion is grounded in published literature on CaBP-CaMKII interactions (Haeseleer et al., 2000) and CaMKII-otoferlin phosphorylation (Meese et al., 2017)
Multiple possible mechanisms are enumerated, showing awareness of complexity
weaknesses: No direct experimental evidence is provided in this paper for CaBP-CaMKII-otoferlin pathway effects
No interaction studies between CaBPs and synaptic proteins were performed
The claim remains entirely speculative with multiple untested links in the proposed chain
alternative_interpretations: The exocytosis deficit beyond QCa reduction could be explained by endocytic changes or changes in vesicle pool sizes unrelated to CaBP-protein interactions
CaBPs could affect exocytosis indirectly through altered intracellular Ca2+ dynamics rather than through direct protein-protein interactions
required_assumptions: CaBPs interact with CaMKII in IHCs
CaMKII phosphorylation of otoferlin is functionally significant in IHC exocytosis
evaluation.notes: This is appropriately presented as a hypothesis for future testing rather than a conclusion, so the 'calibrated' rating reflects the match between claim strength and evidence.

nodes.label: At –55 mV holding potential, maximal Ca2+ currents were reduced by 60 ± 4% in DK…
nodes.claim: At –55 mV holding potential, maximal Ca2+ currents were reduced by 60 ± 4% in DKO vs 25 ± 4% in WT (p < 0.005), and sustained exocytosis was completely abolished in DKO (p < 0.005).
nodes.verbatim_quote: 60 ± 4% vs 25 ± 4% reduction in DKO and WT IHCs, respectively; p < 0.005...resulted in a complete loss of sustained exocytosis

strengths: Physiologically more relevant holding potential (–55 mV) compared to standard –85 mV
Clear quantification of current reduction with appropriate statistics
Demonstrates activity-dependent worsening of phenotype, which is a key insight
Partial rescue by CaBP2 re-expression strengthens the causal link
weaknesses: The sine wave used during capacitance measurements adds additional channel activation that is acknowledged but difficult to precisely quantify
The claim of 'complete loss' of sustained exocytosis should be interpreted with caution—very small responses may be below detection threshold
Sample sizes for these specific conditions are not explicitly stated
alternative_interpretations: At –55 mV, additional channel types or conductances may be activated that confound interpretation
The 'complete loss' of sustained exocytosis could partly reflect depleted vesicle pools due to ongoing activity rather than solely CaV1.3 inactivation
required_assumptions: –55 mV is a reasonable approximation of the IHC resting potential in vivo
The capacitance measurement technique remains reliable at this holding potential
evaluation.notes: This experiment is one of the most compelling in the paper as it bridges in vitro recordings toward in vivo relevance.

nodes.label: Click thresholds were 59 ± 2 dB SPL in DKO (N=9) vs 30 ± 2 dB SPL in WT (N=8) at…
nodes.claim: Click thresholds were 59 ± 2 dB SPL in DKO (N=9) vs 30 ± 2 dB SPL in WT (N=8) at 3–4 weeks, worsening to 68 ± 5 dB SPL at 7–13 weeks.
nodes.verbatim_quote: Click responses were better preserved (thresholds of 59 ± 2 dB SPL in DKO (N = 9) vs 30 ± 2 dB SPL in WT (N = 8) mice)

strengths: Clear, precise threshold measurements with appropriate sample sizes (N=8-9)
Longitudinal data showing progressive worsening strengthens the finding
Click and tone burst stimuli both assessed
Consistent with CaBP2-KO phenotype but more severe, as expected for DKO
weaknesses: Tone burst thresholds assigned 100 dB when exceeding 90 dB maximum, which is a ceiling artifact that may underestimate true threshold elevation
Age groups are somewhat broad (3-4 weeks, 7-13 weeks)
alternative_interpretations: Progressive worsening could partly reflect DPOAE deterioration (OHC function) in some animals rather than purely IHC synaptic dysfunction
required_assumptions: ABR threshold detection methodology is consistent across genotypes
The 10-dB precision of threshold determination is adequate
evaluation.notes: The progressive phenotype is consistent with the in vitro finding of activity-dependent worsening of channel inactivation.

nodes.label: Only 1 out of 20 DKO neurons showed normal tuning curve responses; DKO first spi…
nodes.claim: Only 1 out of 20 DKO neurons showed normal tuning curve responses; DKO first spike latency was 12.5 ± 2.8 ms vs WT 4.8 ± 0.2 ms (p < 0.001), jitter 18.3 ± 5.0 vs WT 1.5 ± 0.4 (p < 0.00001), and adaptation ratio 12.5 ± 3.0 vs WT 3.4 ± 0.2 (p < 0.00001).
nodes.verbatim_quote: only one out of the 20 neurons we recorded and analyzed from DKO animals showed a normal response...increased latency (12.5 ± 2.8 ms vs WT 4.8 ± 0.2 ms; p < 0.001)

strengths: Large sample of WT neurons (n=39) with thorough characterization
DKO sample (n=20) is reasonable for in vivo single-unit recordings
Multiple parameters quantified (latency, jitter, adaptation ratio) with appropriate statistics (Wilcoxon rank-sum test for non-normal distributions)
Very large effect sizes making the findings robust
weaknesses: Only 1/20 DKO neurons showed normal tuning—the extreme nature of this finding introduces potential selection bias (only the most responsive neurons could be found)
The inability to properly classify ~3 DKO units (possible cochlear nucleus neurons) introduces uncertainty
The search stimulus itself (85-90 dB noise bursts) could inactivate DKO CaV1.3 channels, biasing the sample toward less-affected neurons
Three additional units were excluded, which while justified, reduces sample size further
alternative_interpretations: Some recorded DKO units may be cochlear nucleus neurons rather than SGNs, as the authors acknowledge for ~3 units
High thresholds could partly reflect impaired cochlear amplification in some animals rather than solely synaptic dysfunction
required_assumptions: Recording location and spike waveform criteria adequately distinguish SGNs from cochlear nucleus neurons
The search stimulus does not so strongly bias the DKO sample as to make comparisons invalid
evaluation.notes: The authors transparently discuss the experimental challenges and biases inherent in DKO recordings.

nodes.label: DKO SGN responses greatly improved when stimulus repetition rate was lowered fro…
nodes.claim: DKO SGN responses greatly improved when stimulus repetition rate was lowered from 5 Hz to 0.5 Hz, plateauing at 0.2 Hz, consistent with slow CaV1.3 recovery from inactivation being the rate-limiting step.
nodes.verbatim_quote: DKO responses greatly improved when we lowered the stimulus repetition rate to 0.5 Hz, and plateaued at 0.2 Hz.

strengths: Systematic variation of stimulus repetition rate (0.2, 0.5, 5, 10 Hz) provides strong evidence for recovery-rate dependence
Plateau at 0.2 Hz is consistent with the ~5 s recovery time constant from sine wave conditioning experiments
The data directly links in vitro recovery kinetics to in vivo functional consequences
WT comparison shows much faster recovery (mostly recovered by 150 ms), providing internal control
weaknesses: The interpretation that CaV1.3 recovery is the rate-limiting step is plausible but not definitively proven—vesicle replenishment could also contribute
Sample sizes for each stimulus rate condition are not stated
alternative_interpretations: Synaptic vesicle pool depletion and slowed replenishment could also contribute to the rate-dependence of DKO responses
Adaptation mechanisms downstream of the IHC synapse could play a role
required_assumptions: The same neurons were recorded across different repetition rates, or the populations are comparable
CaV1.3 recovery from inactivation is indeed the dominant factor
evaluation.notes: This is one of the strongest translational findings, connecting in vitro channel kinetics to in vivo neural coding. The correlation between recovery time constants from Figure 4 and the rate-dependent improvement is compelling.

nodes.label: DKO animals showed reduced spontaneous spiking activity in SGNs, supporting the …
nodes.claim: DKO animals showed reduced spontaneous spiking activity in SGNs, supporting the hypothesis that even in the absence of sound stimulation a considerable fraction of calcium channels may be in steady-state inactivation.
nodes.verbatim_quote: DKOs also showed reduced spontaneous spiking activity...which supports the hypothesis that already in the absence of sound stimulation over tens of seconds a considerable fraction of calcium channels may be in steady-state inactivation.

strengths: Reduced spontaneous rates are clearly observed in DKO neurons (Figure 7E)
Logical consistency with the hypothesis of steady-state inactivation even at rest
Consistent with the in vitro finding that mild depolarization from –55 mV drives significant inactivation
weaknesses: Severe selection bias: only neurons with some spontaneous or evoked activity could be detected, so the sample likely overrepresents less-affected neurons
Quantitative data on spontaneous rates is presented only graphically (Figure 7E); precise values with statistics are not provided in the text excerpt
Multiple factors could reduce spontaneous rates (e.g., reduced BK channel expression affecting resting potential, synaptic vesicle depletion)
alternative_interpretations: Reduced spontaneous rates could reflect altered IHC resting potential due to BK channel deficiency rather than (or in addition to) CaV1.3 steady-state inactivation
Developmental changes in SGN excitability could contribute
required_assumptions: Spontaneous rate reduction primarily reflects presynaptic CaV1.3 dysfunction rather than other factors
IHC resting potential in vivo drives sufficient CaV1.3 opening to establish steady-state inactivation
evaluation.notes: The interpretation is reasonable but relies on an assumption about the IHC resting potential and its relationship to CaV1.3 activation threshold.

nodes.label: Experimental yield of sound-responsive neurons was much lower in DKO (0.3 per ho…
nodes.claim: Experimental yield of sound-responsive neurons was much lower in DKO (0.3 per hour vs 2.5 in WT), suggesting many DKO neurons failed to generate spontaneous and evoked action potentials.
nodes.verbatim_quote: On average we hit 0.3 sound-responsive neurons per hour of recording, compared to 2.5 in WT. Very likely many DKO neurons failed to generate spontaneous and evoked action potentials

strengths: Striking quantitative difference (0.3 vs 2.5 neurons/hour) is a large and meaningful effect
Consistent with the overall phenotype of severely impaired synaptic transmission
weaknesses: This is an observational metric inherently confounded by multiple factors (electrode placement, animal health under anesthesia, surgical quality)

The interpretation that 'many DKO neurons failed to generate spontaneous and evoked action potentials' is a reasonable hypothesis but cannot be definitively distinguished from neurons being present but undetectable due to methodological limitations
Anesthesia could differentially affect DKO animals
alternative_interpretations: Lower yield could partly reflect differences in cochlear anatomy, nerve accessibility, or animal health rather than solely reflecting absent neural activity
Some neurons may fire but at rates too low to detect with the search stimulus paradigm
required_assumptions: Recording technique and electrode targeting were comparable between WT and DKO experiments
The search stimulus adequately probes for responsive neurons in both genotypes
evaluation.notes: The authors appropriately flag this as an experimental observation with the caveat about causation. The phrasing 'very likely' is suitably cautious.

nodes.label: DPOAEs were normal in about half of DKO animals, and reduced but still detectabl…
nodes.claim: DPOAEs were normal in about half of DKO animals, and reduced but still detectable in the other half, in both age groups tested.
nodes.verbatim_quote: In about half of the DKO animals in both age groups, the DPOAEs were normal. In the other half, they were reduced in amplitude but still detectable

strengths: Both DPOAE thresholds and amplitude growth functions assessed
Multiple frequency combinations tested
Individual animal data presented, showing the variability explicitly
weaknesses: Approximately half of DKO animals showing reduced DPOAEs complicates the interpretation—is this OHC dysfunction or middle ear pathology?
Different setups with different calibrations were used for the two age groups, limiting direct comparison
Statistical significance was reached at 7-13 weeks (p < 0.002, two-way ANOVA), suggesting some OHC involvement with age
The variability within the DKO group weakens the claim of 'largely preserved' cochlear amplification
alternative_interpretations: The DPOAE reduction in half of DKO animals could indicate CaBP1/2 effects on OHC function or cochlear homeostasis
Middle ear effects from the genetic background or surgery (in injected animals) could contribute
CaBP expression in OHCs, if present, could directly affect OHC function
required_assumptions: DPOAEs adequately reflect OHC function
CaBP1 and 2 are not significantly expressed in OHCs
evaluation.notes: The authors' claim of 'largely preserved' cochlear amplification is reasonable for the younger age group but becomes more tenuous at older ages.

nodes.label: Both RibeyeA/CtBP2 and Homer1 immunofluorescence intensities were significantly …
nodes.claim: Both RibeyeA/CtBP2 and Homer1 immunofluorescence intensities were significantly higher in DKO (p < 0.005, Wilcoxon rank-sum test; 614 WT vs 441 DKO immunospots analyzed).
nodes.verbatim_quote: A significantly higher immunofluorescence intensity was observed for pre- (RibeyeA or CtBP2) and postsynaptic (Homer1) markers in Cabp1/2-DKO mice (analysis of 614 and 441 immunospots from WT and Cabp1/2-DKO organs of Corti, respectively; N = 5 for both genotypes; asterisks; Wilcoxon rank-sum test, p < 0.005)

strengths: Large sample sizes (614 WT vs 441 DKO immunospots)
N=5 organs per genotype, processed in parallel—appropriate experimental design
Appropriate non-parametric test (Wilcoxon rank-sum) used
Both pre- and postsynaptic markers show the same trend, suggesting coordinated synaptic changes
Consistent with compensatory changes seen in other synaptic mutants (Eckrich et al., 2019; Kim et al., 2019)
weaknesses: Immunofluorescence intensity is semi-quantitative and can be influenced by tissue processing, antibody penetration, and imaging parameters
Parallel processing mitigates but does not eliminate batch effects
Increased intensity does not necessarily indicate increased protein levels—conformational changes or accessibility could affect antibody binding
alternative_interpretations: Increased immunofluorescence could reflect larger synaptic structures rather than compensatory protein upregulation
Changes could be secondary to altered neural activity patterns rather than a direct effect of CaBP loss
required_assumptions: Immunofluorescence intensity correlates with protein abundance
Tissue processing was truly equivalent between genotypes
evaluation.notes: The finding is consistent with homeostatic synaptic plasticity in response to reduced postsynaptic activity.

nodes.label: BK-cluster volume per IHC was 6.6 ± 1.1 µm³ in DKO vs 14.2 ± 2.1 µm³ in WT (p < …
nodes.claim: BK-cluster volume per IHC was 6.6 ± 1.1 µm³ in DKO vs 14.2 ± 2.1 µm³ in WT (p < 0.01); individual cluster volumes also significantly smaller (p < 0.0001).
nodes.verbatim_quote: cumulative 'volume' of BK-cluster immunofluorescence per IHC, which was significantly higher in WT IHCs, indicating higher abundance of BK channels (14.2 ± 2.1 vs 6.6 ± 1.1 µm3 per IHC, Student's t-test, p < 0.01)

strengths: Quantitative 3D analysis using Imaris software for volume measurements
Both individual cluster volumes (p < 0.0001) and cumulative volume per IHC (p < 0.01) reported
N=6 organs per genotype—reasonable sample size
Partial reversal by CaBP2 re-expression supports functional link
Worsening with age (more obvious at 14 weeks) consistent with progressive phenotype
weaknesses: Immunofluorescence 'volume' is a proxy for protein abundance, not a direct measure
The mechanism linking CaBP1/2 loss to BK channel reduction is entirely speculative ('CaBPs may directly regulate BK expression')
Cannot distinguish between reduced BK expression and altered BK trafficking/clustering
alternative_interpretations: Reduced BK clustering could be a secondary effect of altered Ca2+ homeostasis rather than a direct CaBP function
Similar BK reduction seen in other CaV1.3 mutants (Brandt et al., 2003) suggests this is downstream of Ca2+ signaling disruption, not a specific CaBP effect
required_assumptions: Imaris volume measurements reliably reflect BK channel abundance
BK immunofluorescence conditions were comparable between genotypes
evaluation.notes: The authors appropriately consider both direct and indirect mechanisms. The observation is consistent with the broader literature on Ca2+-dependent regulation of BK expression in IHCs.

nodes.label: CaBP2 is the most abundant CaBP family member in the cochlea, followed by CaBP1;…
nodes.claim: CaBP2 is the most abundant CaBP family member in the cochlea, followed by CaBP1; CaBP4 and CaBP5 levels are negligible.
nodes.verbatim_quote: The murine cochlea shows strong expression of CaBP1 and 2, while the levels of CaBP4 and 5 seem negligible

strengths: Supported by referenced prior literature (Yang et al., 2016; Jean et al., 2023; Xu et al., 2022)
Consistent with the biological rationale for studying CaBP1/2 DKO specifically
weaknesses: No new expression data generated in this study; relies entirely on previously published work
Some cited references assess mRNA expression, which may not perfectly correlate with protein levels

The statement about CaBP2 being 'most abundant' vs CaBP1 is somewhat equivocal in the text ('CaBP2, followed by the structurally similar CaBP1, are the most abundant'), and another sentence says CaBP1 and 2 show 'strong expression' without directly ranking them
alternative_interpretations: mRNA expression levels may not reflect functional protein abundance at the synapse
required_assumptions: Prior expression studies accurately reflect the relative abundance of CaBP family members in the cochlea
Protein levels correlate with mRNA levels
evaluation.notes: This is background information rather than a novel finding. The claim is well-supported by cited literature.

nodes.label: Fraction of remaining Ca2+ current after 500-ms depolarization was significantly…
nodes.claim: Fraction of remaining Ca2+ current after 500-ms depolarization was significantly improved upon CaBP2 re-expression (p < 0.0001), and Ca2+ currents upon train stimuli were efficiently rescued.
nodes.verbatim_quote: Ca2+ currents were greatly reduced upon application of short train stimuli and rescued efficiently by the introduction of the transgenic CaBP2

strengths: Quantitative comparison with highly significant p-value (p < 0.0001) for inactivation rescue
Multiple stimulus paradigms (500-ms step and train stimuli) show consistent rescue
Rescue is partial, which is transparently reported and discussed
weaknesses: The train stimulus data is noted to come from cells with lower-than-average inactivation (0.36 vs 0.47), potentially overestimating rescue efficacy for this measure
Incomplete rescue leaves open the question of whether CaBP1 absence prevents full recovery, or whether CaBP2 expression levels are inadequate
The viral delivery approach introduces variability in transduction efficiency across cells
alternative_interpretations: Partial rescue could reflect inadequate transgene expression levels rather than irreversible adaptations or CaBP1-specific functions
The specific CaBP2 isoform used (L-isoform rather than CaBP2-alt) may not optimally rescue all functions
required_assumptions: Transgenic CaBP2 expression is sufficiently uniform across recorded IHCs
The CaBP2 L-isoform used can substitute for native CaBP2-alt function
evaluation.notes: The authors discuss the isoform issue (L vs alt) and acknowledge incomplete rescue openly.

nodes.label: ABR thresholds in injected DKO ears were significantly improved for all tone bur…
nodes.claim: ABR thresholds in injected DKO ears were significantly improved for all tone burst frequencies and click stimuli (p values in Supplementary file 1), and ABR wave I amplitude strongly recovered (p ≤ 0.0001 for DKO vs WT or vs injected DKO).
nodes.verbatim_quote: A strong recovery of the amplitude of the ABR wave I (asterisks, Tukey's multicomparison test; p ≤ 0.0001 for DKO vs WT or vs injected DKO)

strengths: Comprehensive assessment: thresholds, wave I amplitude, and latency all show improvement
Highly significant rescue of wave I amplitude (p ≤ 0.0001)
Summated wave I-IV responses not distinguishable from WT (Figure 6—figure supplement 2C)
Consistent with cellular-level rescue data (Ca2+ currents, exocytosis)
Appropriate multiple comparison correction (Tukey's test)
weaknesses: Thresholds did not completely recover to WT levels, indicating partial rescue
eGFP expression was lower toward the cochlear base, which may correlate with incomplete threshold recovery at higher frequencies
Contralateral ear also showed some eGFP expression, which could confound comparisons if contralateral ears were used as controls
